memoryText: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Job 28:28 several times, and then try to say it without looking. Read the meditation and the week in review, and then choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or discuss with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Job 28:28 is the answer to a question that the whole poem has been asking: where can wisdom be found? After describing all the things human beings can discover, the poem gives a single, simple verse.

“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.” The word “fear” does not mean terror. It means reverence, awe, and a settled sense that God is God and you are not. It is the posture of a creature before the Creator. To fear the Lord is to take him seriously, to take his words seriously, and to let him be the final authority in your life. It is the starting point of all true knowledge.

“And to turn away from evil is understanding.” Here wisdom becomes practical. Understanding is not first about having correct information. It is about the direction of your life. It is a turning. The wise person is not the one who has solved every puzzle but the one who walks away from what is wrong, even when it is costly.

Notice that neither half of the verse claims to explain suffering. This is the wisdom Job needs. He cannot solve the puzzle. But he can fear God and turn from evil, and that is what the narrator said about him in 1:1. The book keeps coming back to that.

For the Christian, this wisdom has a face. Jesus is the wisdom of God. To fear the Lord is to come to Christ, and to turn from evil is to follow him.
weekInReview: This week you read the last of the debates and the beginning of God’s answer. You heard Job describe the oppression of the poor and ask why God does not seem to act, and you heard him praise God’s power as only the outskirts of his ways. You read the great poem on wisdom in chapter 28 and Job’s vow of integrity. You read Job’s long final defense, in which he remembered his better days, described his present pain, and swore that he had not wronged anyone. Then Elihu spoke. He said some wise things and made some mistakes, and he ended with a storm. In the last reading of the week, God answered Job out of the whirlwind with questions about the world he has made. The week taught that wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, and that God answers not with explanations but with his own greatness.
reflectionQuestions: Chapter 28 says that wisdom cannot be bought or mined. Where have you been looking for wisdom? What would it mean for you to begin with the fear of the Lord this week?

How does Jesus, who is the wisdom of God and who came as a man of suffering, show you what the fear of the Lord and turning from evil look like in practice? Think of one scene from the Gospels where you see this clearly.
God answered Job with questions about creation rather than answers about suffering. What question do you most want God to answer? What would it mean to trust him with it?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you the fear of the Lord.
Thank him that Jesus is the wisdom of God.
Rest in his greatness this Sabbath.
